newsitem.title: BELGIUM: 1998 budgets to count for EMU test too - Lamfalussy.
newsitem.headline: 1998 budgets to count for EMU test too - Lamfalussy.

text.p: The selection of countries to take part in a single European currency will depend on 1998 budgets as well as 1997 budgets, European Monetary Institute (EMI) President Alexandre Lamfalussy reiterated in an interview with a Belgian newspaper published on Saturday.
"Public finances can still be corrected in 1997. Long term reforms are also important, notably the preparation of the 1998 budget as of now," he told the Financieel Economische Tijd.
"The 1998 budget can not correct a bad 1997 budget, but it can confirm a good 1997 budget," he added.

The single currency is scheduled to be introduced on January 1, 1999, with contenders to take part due to be picked early next year on the basis of 1997 data and partially on the basis of recommendations submitted by the EMI.

The issue of sustainable fulfilment of the convergence criteria has gained in significance in recent months as more and more signs emerge that key European Union countries will struggle to meet the Maastricht criteria on the nail.

Asked if Germany would meet the criteria, Lamfalussy said, "Germany says the rise of its state debt is due to exceptional circumstances, notably unification. They have a point. But this does not count for the budget deficit."

"I repeat that the Maastricht treaty says three things about budget criteria. First there are the reference levels of three percent (of gross domestic product) for deficit, 60 percent for debt. Secondly the treaty allows for unquantified divergences from these...levels. Thirdly state finances must be tenable.
"Therefore not only the results of 1997 are important, but also the 1998 budgets."
He said if Germany made serious efforts which led to its deficit falling in a durable manner, then after about two years its debt would start to fall as well.
Asked which was more important if a choice had to be made between convergence or introducing a single currency on time, Lamfalussy said a delay of one or two months would be acceptable.
"I agree with Bundesbank President (Hans) Tietmeyer that one or two months' delay for technical reasons would be no problem.
"But a longer delay, by one or two years would be very dangerous because then there is the risk that confidence is lost," he said, adding that to speculate now about a delay was counter-productive.
